evidence:
PLAN (avoided): Section 0 pins the fact pattern before any inference — 'the idea as stated contains three unverified assumptions: that a guarantee existed, that it was *removed* rather than *released on a pre-agreed schedule*, and that the hyperscaler's economic commitment changed as a result.' H0 is explicitly the base case, not a strawman: 'The guarantee release was pre-negotiated at inception, triggered automatically by a completion test, DSCR test, or ratings/leverage condition, or was removed for accounting reasons — to avoid a guarantee liability under ASC 460, to avoid consolidating the SPV as a VIE under ASC 810, or to keep the obligation out of the contractual obligations table. Economic commitment unchanged.' The seasoning-as-strength reading is H3: 'The SPV became standalone-financeable — construction complete, third-party customers added, subsidy tranche received ... and lenders no longer required the credit enhancement.' Section 9 states the trap in one line: 'The dominant error is conflating a legal guarantee with an economic commitment.' Base rates in Section 5, independent second-source evidence in Section 4, pre-committed kill criteria in Section 8. Gap: the negotiated/consented-by-the-provider point (gold (c)) is never argued — the plan tests whether commitment changed, not whether the chip maker agreed to the release.

CRITIQUE (caught): It names the financing-not-sourcing reading squarely — 'what you are looking at is a term that changed between a marketing term sheet, a commitment letter, and executed docs — a negotiation artifact, driven by lender appetite, rating agency treatment, and parent-level debt capacity, not by silicon roadmaps.' It presses the consolidation test as decisive and cheap: 'Dropping a parent guarantee does not by itself avoid VIE consolidation — the analysis turns on power over significant activities plus variable interests, and a take-or-pay capacity reservation is itself a variable interest that can force consolidation'; 'if the hyperscaler's filings show it does not consolidate the SPV, that meaningfully constrains how much economic commitment can be hiding elsewhere. That is a cheap, decisive test buried in a footnote reference' — and promotes it to the half-day screen: 'Does the hyperscaler consolidate the SPV, and did that change? (30 min).' It caught the negotiated character on the lender/agency side and priced the prior accordingly: 'Guarantee structures are set by treasury and capital markets people negotiating with lenders and rating agencies, frequently with no line of sight into the product org's sourcing roadmap. The plan assumes this decision encodes sourcing intent. Absent a stated mechanism, the honest prior on H1 as the unique explanation is 5–10%, not the 30–40% the resource allocation implies.' It adds the mirror-image bullish hypothesis: 'The guarantee may have come off because the program *grew* past the point where the parent wanted the obligation on its balance sheet ... Bigger commitment, less disclosure.' What it does not say: that the chip maker itself consented to the release, which is the direct refutation of 'pushing risk back onto their primary provider.' Lenders are named; the counterparty's agreement is not.
missed: The counterparty consented. A guarantor release requires the SPV's lenders AND the chip maker to sign the amendment — the provider agreed to it. That single fact guts the 'pushing risk back onto their primary provider' framing (it is bilateral, not unilateral), and it is almost certainly compensated somewhere: wider spread on the SPV debt, a fee, a pricing concession in the offtake, or a tighter covenant package. The critique reprices the sourcing inference but never dismantles the 'pushing risk' half of the seed.

The right base rate is never supplied. The critique cuts the case book to 3-5 analogues but does not replace it with the relevant frequency: in project/asset-backed SPV finance, sponsor completion support is *conventionally* released on a completion or performance test, and releases at first refinancing are close to routine. If the unconditional release rate at seasoning is high, the event carries near-zero information and nothing downstream matters. 'Cut the case book' without stating the counterfactual leaves the project with no null denominator.

Seasoning-as-strength is not pressed as the live alternative conclusion. The plan has H3 and the critique adds a bullish H6 about off-balance-sheet disclosure, but neither states the cleaner inverse: if the SPV's assets have seasoned to where the structure carries its own credit unsupported, the correct read on the primary provider is constructive, and the recommended short leg is exactly backwards. A desk would ask for the SPV's standalone metrics — utilization, contracted cash flows, DSCR, third-party offtake share — before letting anyone short on this.

No cross-sectional test within the sponsor. Cheapest available base rate: has this hyperscaler released or declined to give guarantees on its *other* SPVs and JVs over the same period? A treasury-policy shift shows up across vehicles at once and has nothing to do with any one supplier. That is an afternoon of filings work and it is a cleaner control than 22 hand-picked cross-company cases.

The mirror-image accounting question on the supplier is unasked. If the hyperscaler deconsolidates, someone else may consolidate — check whether the SPV moved onto the chip maker's balance sheet, what it did to that entity's leverage, net debt, and covenant headroom, and whether the manufacturer's own filings or agency reports explain the release. That is where a real, tradeable credit consequence would live, and it is absent from both documents.

Falsification is inherited, not sharpened. The critique never adds the affirmative second-source tests with dates attached — foundry/ASIC qualification disclosures, tape-out and NRE timing, mask-set and prepayment terms, supply-agreement amendments — nor states the window after which the absence of them retires the idea. It kills the project on cost and consensus grounds, which is not the same as saying what evidence would prove the thesis wrong.

Covenant and refinancing mechanics go untested. Ratings-agency methodology changes, a parent rating action, ASC 460 recognition thresholds, or a lender-side change-of-control/leverage covenant at refi can each force a guarantee off with zero strategic content. The critique gestures at 'rating agency treatment' but never turns it into a testable list — which is the shortest path from 'probably financing' to 'demonstrably financing.'
manufactured: 'BMP and Corrado are cross-sectional tests; you don't have a cross-section.' This misreads the plan. Section 6 assigns those tests to the base-rate sample explicitly — 'For the base-rate sample, use the Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen standardized cross-sectional test, with the Corrado rank test as a non-parametric robustness check given small n' — not to the single name. The n=1 CAR objection stands; the statistics objection is against something the plan did not say.

'That means "removed for accounting reasons" and H2 "replaced by an economically equivalent take-or-pay" are partly mutually exclusive.' Overdrawn. ASC 460 guarantee-liability recognition and ASC 810 consolidation are separate motives, and a take-or-pay is a variable interest only on its terms (pricing, residual-value and utilization risk absorbed); many capacity reservations are not. Manufacturing a contradiction between H0 and H2 also mildly undercuts the very accounting null the critique elsewhere wants promoted.

'Customs/Panjiva. The plan correctly says it can never be primary evidence, then still budgets licensing and days for it. Drop it.' The plan never allocates days or a licensing line to customs data — it names it inside one corroboration channel and pre-emptively demotes it ('use these as corroboration, never as primary evidence'). Criticising the plan for a budget it did not make, then telling it to do what it already did.
'It is also over-scoped by roughly 3x against its own timeline.' Asserted, never derived. The 3x is a number with no working behind it, and it is doing real load-bearing work in the verdict.
verdict_line: Plan gets the null right — SPV guarantee release is a deconsolidation/financing fact until proven otherwise — and the critique correctly reprices H1 to single digits and promotes the consolidation check to hour one; but nobody says the obvious thing, which is that the chip maker signed the release itself, so 'pushing risk onto the provider' is dead on arrival, and nobody produces the base rate for how routine sponsor-support releases are at seasoning — cut the case book and the event study, keep the Taiwan monthly revenue monitor, don't put on the short.
